relevant_findings.topic: Dual-substrate spec — concrete and wood porch floors share horizontal exposure but diverge on prep and coating
relevant_findings.finding: Porch and patio floors encompass two fundamentally different substrates: (1) Poured concrete — alkaline (pH 12-14), requires CSP profiling and moisture testing, coated with film-forming or penetrating concrete coatings. (2) Wood porch decking — organic, requires MC verification (< 15%), coated with porch enamel (film-forming paint). The substrate_type dimension (concrete vs wood) is the primary branch point that drives completely different prep modules, primer systems, coating systems, and failure mode profiles. Despite these differences, both share horizontal surface characteristics: foot traffic abrasion, water pooling, UV exposure, and mandatory slip resistance.

relevant_findings.topic: Coating system is the primary configuration dimension — NOT quality tier
relevant_findings.finding: Like the deck staining spec (SF_DECK_EXT_v1), coating_system replaces quality_tier as the primary dimension. For concrete: porch_enamel (traditional acrylic porch & floor paint), concrete_stain (penetrating decorative), acrylic_sealer (breathable film), polyurea (extreme durability, fast return to service). For wood: porch_enamel is the dominant and traditional coating. Each coating system drives different surface prep requirements, primer selection, application method, cure time, and maintenance cycle. Quality tier is subordinate — it modifies execution precision within a given coating system.
relevant_findings.source: Exterior_Concrete_Masonry_Floors_Doctrine.md §1; Researcher analysis of sibling spec SF_DECK_EXT_v1

relevant_findings.topic: Epoxy excluded from v1 scope for exterior porch/patio
relevant_findings.finding: Standard epoxy systems are EXCLUDED from this spec's v1 coating_system options. Aromatic epoxies yellow and chalk rapidly under UV exposure. While epoxy + UV-stable topcoat is technically viable, it is primarily an interior garage floor or industrial application. Residential exterior porch/patio use does not justify the complexity of a two-component epoxy + polyurethane topcoat system. Polyurea/polyaspartic provides superior UV stability, faster cure, and better freeze-thaw resistance without requiring a separate UV topcoat — it is the correct high-performance option for exterior residential floors.

relevant_findings.topic: Surface preparation is 80% of coating longevity on concrete
relevant_findings.finding: Concrete surface profile (CSP) is the single most critical factor in coating adhesion and longevity. Three prep methods map to coating systems: (1) Acid etch → CSP 1 (light profile) — suitable for thin acrylics and penetrating stains. (2) Diamond grind → CSP 2-3 — required for porch enamel and polyurea systems. Production: 500-1,000 SF/hr. (3) Shot blast → CSP 3-5 — heavy-duty industrial, overkill for residential porch but available. Production: 1,500-3,000 SF/hr. Laitance (weak dusty surface layer) and form-release agents MUST be removed — they are the primary cause of delamination on new concrete.

relevant_findings.topic: Moisture testing is mandatory for concrete substrates — hard stop thresholds
relevant_findings.finding: Hydrostatic moisture pressure is a leading cause of coating failure on concrete floors. Two standard tests: (1) Calcium Chloride ASTM F1869 — MVER must be < 3-5 lbs/1,000 SF/24 hrs. (2) In-Situ RH ASTM F2170 — internal slab RH must be < 75-85%. If moisture exceeds limits, it is a HARD STOP — moisture-mitigating primer is required before any coating can be applied. Impermeable coatings (polyurea, epoxy) applied over wet concrete will suffer osmotic blistering as trapped moisture vapor pushes through the slab and lifts the coating film.

relevant_findings.topic: Slip resistance is MANDATORY for exterior horizontal surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: All exterior porch/patio floor coatings must meet slip resistance standards: ANSI DCOF >= 0.55 for exterior wet areas, OSHA SCOF >= 0.5 for walkways and >= 0.8 for ramps. Anti-slip aggregates are required: silica sand for level walkway surfaces, aluminum oxide or carborundum for steps and ramps (extreme hardness, long-term abrasion resistance). Application methods: suspended in final coat mix or broadcast into wet coating to refusal. Anti-slip aggregate is an auto-add task when the surface includes steps or ramps.

relevant_findings.topic: Wood porch floors use porch enamel — distinct from deck stain
relevant_findings.finding: Wood porch floors are traditionally coated with porch & floor enamel (alkyd or acrylic porch paint), NOT deck stain. Porch enamel is a film-forming paint that provides a hard, glossy, abrasion-resistant surface suitable for foot traffic. This is fundamentally different from the penetrating stain systems used on open decks. Porch enamel requires: proper surface prep (mill glaze removal on new wood), primer on bare wood, and 2 finish coats. The film-forming nature of porch enamel means moisture management is critical — porches are typically covered, which reduces but does not eliminate water exposure.
relevant_findings.source: Exterior_Decks_Horizontal_Wood_Doctrine.md; field convention — porch enamel is the traditional wood porch coating

relevant_findings.topic: New wood porch requires mill glaze removal and MC verification
relevant_findings.finding: New wood porch decking (typically tongue-and-groove fir, pine, or PT pine) has mill glaze from high-speed planing that blocks coating adhesion. Mill glaze removal is mandatory via chemical remover or 60-80 grit sanding. Moisture content must be verified at < 15% before coating. New PT lumber requires 3-6 month seasoning. These requirements parallel the deck spec but the coating system is porch enamel (paint) rather than penetrating stain, so primer is required on bare wood.

relevant_findings.topic: Concrete alkalinity drives primer selection on new construction
relevant_findings.finding: New poured concrete is highly alkaline (pH 12-14) from Portland cement hydration. Standard acrylic paints fail on uncured alkaline concrete — alkali burn destroys latex binders. For porch enamel on concrete: alkali-resistant primer (e.g., SW Loxon Masonry Primer) is MANDATORY on bare concrete. For acrylic sealers: most are formulated to tolerate alkaline substrates directly. For polyurea: manufacturer-specific primer/basecoat over profiled concrete. The 28-day cure ideal is rarely achievable on NC schedules — accelerated coating at 7+ days with alkali-resistant primer is the standard NC path.

relevant_findings.topic: Horizontal surfaces face multi-axial assault vs vertical surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Porch and patio floors endure conditions that vertical surfaces do not: (1) Water pooling — horizontal surfaces do not shed water, leading to chronic moisture saturation and hydrostatic pressure. (2) Foot traffic abrasion — constant mechanical wear from shoes, pets, furniture dragging. (3) Direct overhead UV — maximum solar radiation intensity. (4) Freeze-thaw cycling — pooled water in cracks expands 9% when freezing, spalling concrete and shattering coating films. These factors combine to produce dramatically shorter coating lifecycles than vertical exterior surfaces and mandate higher-performance coating systems.

relevant_findings.topic: Polyurea/polyaspartic is the premium concrete porch coating
relevant_findings.finding: Polyurea and polyaspartic coatings offer: excellent UV stability, extreme abrasion resistance, moderate vapor permeability, fast cure (1-6 hours to return to service), and excellent freeze-thaw resistance. They are the correct high-performance option for exterior residential concrete floors where durability justifies the higher material cost. Fast cure time is particularly valuable for porches where homeowner access disruption must be minimized. Polyurea requires CSP 2-3 (diamond grind) surface prep and manufacturer-specific primer/basecoat.

relevant_findings.topic: Acrylic sealers are breathable — key advantage for moisture-prone slabs
relevant_findings.finding: Acrylic sealers have high vapor permeability (breathable), allowing moisture vapor transmission through the coating film. This is a critical advantage on concrete porches where subgrade moisture may be present but MVER is within acceptable limits. Acrylic sealers avoid the osmotic blistering risk that impermeable coatings face. Trade-off: acrylic sealers have low abrasion resistance and shorter lifecycle (2-4 years on horizontal surfaces). Best for light residential use where breathability is more important than extreme durability.

relevant_findings.topic: Scope limited to porch/patio — NOT driveways
relevant_findings.finding: This spec is scoped to residential porch floors and patio surfaces — pedestrian walking surfaces only. Driveways are EXCLUDED because they introduce hot tire pickup as a dominant failure mode (vehicle tire heat softens coating, cooling tire peels coating off concrete). Driveway coating requires polyurea or high-solids epoxy specifically engineered for hot tire resistance. Pool decks are also excluded — they have separate chemical exposure requirements (chlorine, salt) and enhanced slip resistance standards. A future SF_DRIVEWAY_EXT_v1 or SF_POOL_DECK_EXT_v1 could address those scopes.

relevant_findings.topic: Covered vs uncovered porch affects exposure and coating selection
relevant_findings.finding: Covered porches (roof overhead) have reduced UV exposure, reduced water pooling, and reduced freeze-thaw cycling compared to open patios. This affects coating selection: covered porches can use porch enamel or acrylic sealer with reasonable longevity. Open patios face full weather exposure and benefit from polyurea or heavier-duty acrylic systems. Covered/uncovered is a modifier on maintenance cycle expectations and coating system recommendation, but does not change the task structure.

condition_drivers.impact: PRIMARY BRANCH DIMENSION. Drives completely different prep modules (CSP profiling vs mill glaze removal), primer systems (alkali-resistant masonry primer vs wood primer), coating systems (acrylic sealer/concrete stain/polyurea vs porch enamel), moisture testing protocols (ASTM F1869/F2170 vs pin meter MC), and failure mode profiles. A project selects one substrate_type — mixed substrates would be scoped as separate areas.
condition_drivers.notes: Concrete is the dominant NC porch substrate. Wood porch decking is traditional/regional (New England, Southern porches).

condition_drivers.impact: PRIMARY CONFIGURATION DIMENSION (within substrate_type). Drives surface prep method (acid etch vs diamond grind), primer type, application method, cure time, slip resistance approach, and maintenance cycle. Porch_enamel applies to BOTH concrete and wood substrates. Concrete_stain, acrylic_sealer, and polyurea apply to concrete substrate only.
condition_drivers.notes: Porch_enamel is the traditional residential standard for both concrete and wood porches. Polyurea is the premium option for concrete.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives primer requirement and prep sequence. SS_EXT_BARE_MASONRY: new poured concrete requiring alkali-resistant primer. SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD: new wood porch decking requiring wood primer. Both are NC-only states.
condition_drivers.notes: NC spec — only bare substrate states. Repaint states (previously coated concrete/wood) would be a separate spec.

condition_drivers.impact: Modifier on coating system recommendation and maintenance cycle expectations. Covered porches have reduced UV, water, and freeze-thaw exposure. Open patios face full weather assault. Does NOT change task structure — treated as a modifier/advisory, not a workflow branch.
condition_drivers.notes: Covered vs uncovered affects recommendation strength but both paths use the same task sequence.

condition_drivers.impact: When true, auto-adds anti-slip aggregate task for step treads. Steps require aluminum oxide or carborundum aggregate (not just silica sand). Step count drives EA-based tasks for edge detail work and aggregate application.
condition_drivers.notes: Boolean flag. Steps on a porch are common (entry stairs). Slip resistance on steps is a safety-critical requirement.

condition_drivers.impact: Roll is primary for floor field (large flat horizontal surface). Brush_roll for edges, steps, and small areas. Spray_backroll for large open patios (spray deposits coating, backroll forces into surface profile on concrete). Roller nap: 3/8-1/2 inch for smooth concrete, 3/4 inch for textured/broom-finished concrete.
condition_drivers.notes: Spray-only is NOT acceptable on concrete floors (same as masonry — must backroll). Wood porch enamel can be brush/roll or spray_backroll.

quality_differences.description: Traditional porch & floor paint. Film-forming acrylic or alkyd enamel. Hard, glossy, abrasion-resistant surface. Available for both concrete and wood substrates. 2 finish coats over primer. 5-7 year maintenance cycle on covered porches, 3-5 years on open patios. Classic look — the standard residential porch floor treatment for decades.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard residential porches (concrete or wood). Covered front porches. Traditional porch aesthetic.

quality_differences.description: Penetrating decorative stain for concrete. Acid stains react with calcium hydroxide for mottled, variegated color. Water-based stains provide more uniform color. No film formation — requires topcoat sealer for protection. Decorative focus rather than protection focus.
quality_differences.typical_use: Decorative concrete patios. Homeowner wants natural/artistic concrete look. Requires clear sealer topcoat.

quality_differences.description: Breathable film-forming sealer. High vapor permeability — allows moisture vapor transmission. Low abrasion resistance. 2-4 hour cure. 2-4 year maintenance cycle on horizontal surfaces. Best for light residential use where breathability is the priority over durability. Lowest material cost.
quality_differences.typical_use: Light-use patios. Concrete porches with suspected subgrade moisture. Budget-conscious residential.

quality_differences.description: Premium high-performance coating. Excellent UV stability, extreme abrasion resistance, fast cure (1-6 hours return to service), excellent freeze-thaw resistance. Requires diamond grind CSP 2-3 surface prep. Highest material cost. 7-10+ year maintenance cycle.
quality_differences.typical_use: High-end residential patios. Freeze-thaw climate zones. Homeowner wants maximum durability and minimal maintenance. Open patios with full weather exposure.

failure_modes.name: Delamination from insufficient surface profile
failure_modes.description: Coating applied to smooth, unpropped concrete (no CSP) or concrete with laitance/form-release agents delaminates in sheets. The coating has no mechanical bond to the substrate. This is the #1 failure mode on concrete floors and is entirely preventable with proper surface preparation.
failure_modes.prevention: Achieve correct CSP per coating system: CSP 1 for stains/thin acrylics, CSP 2-3 for porch enamel and polyurea. Remove all laitance, form-release agents, oils, and curing compounds before coating.
failure_modes.detection: Coating lifts in sheets or large flakes. Adhesion test failure. Smooth, shiny concrete visible under peeled coating.

failure_modes.name: Osmotic blistering from trapped moisture
failure_modes.description: Impermeable coating (polyurea, porch enamel) applied over concrete with excessive subgrade moisture. Moisture vapor migrates through the slab, hits the impermeable coating, and creates osmotic pressure that pushes the coating off from underneath. Appears as large blisters filled with milky liquid.
failure_modes.prevention: Perform moisture testing before coating: ASTM F1869 MVER < 3-5 lbs/1,000 SF/24 hrs, ASTM F2170 RH < 75-85%. If exceeds limits, apply moisture-mitigating primer before coating. Consider breathable acrylic sealer as alternative for borderline moisture conditions.
failure_modes.detection: Dome-shaped blisters on coating surface. Milky or clear liquid under blisters. Blisters concentrated in areas with poor drainage or high water table.

failure_modes.name: Alkali burn on uncured concrete
failure_modes.description: Standard acrylic paint or porch enamel applied directly to new concrete (pH 12-14) without alkali-resistant primer. Alkaline hydroxides saponify the paint binder — the coating softens, discolors, blisters, and detaches. Complete coating failure requiring full removal.
failure_modes.prevention: ALWAYS use alkali-resistant primer on bare new concrete. Allow minimum 7 days concrete cure before coating (28 days ideal). Test surface pH if cure time is uncertain.
failure_modes.detection: Soft, sticky paint film. Paint easily removed by fingernail. Yellow-brown discoloration. Soap-like residue on surface.

failure_modes.name: Freeze-thaw spalling
failure_modes.description: Water pooled in cracks and surface pores of concrete freezes and expands 9%, fracturing the concrete surface and shattering the coating film above it. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles progressively destroy the surface. Most severe on open patios in northern climates.
failure_modes.prevention: Ensure proper surface drainage (slope away from structure). Seal all cracks before coating. Use flexible coating systems (polyurea) in freeze-thaw zones. Acrylic sealers offer moderate freeze-thaw tolerance due to breathability.
failure_modes.detection: Surface flaking and pitting. Coating peeling in areas around cracks. Progressive surface deterioration after winter seasons.

failure_modes.name: Premature wear from foot traffic abrasion
failure_modes.description: Coatings with low abrasion resistance (acrylic sealers, thin concrete stains without topcoat) wear through quickly in high-traffic paths (doorway thresholds, stair nosings, furniture drag paths). Horizontal walking surfaces experience dramatically more abrasion than vertical surfaces.
failure_modes.prevention: Match coating system to traffic level: acrylic sealer for light use only, porch enamel for standard residential, polyurea for heavy traffic. Anti-slip aggregate also adds abrasion resistance to the surface. Apply full recommended DFT — thin coats fail faster.
failure_modes.detection: Worn pathways showing bare substrate. Color loss in high-traffic areas. Coating thinner at doorway transitions and stair nosings.

failure_modes.name: Porch enamel peeling on wood from moisture entrapment
failure_modes.description: Film-forming porch enamel on wood porch decking traps moisture from rain splash, snow melt, or subfloor condensation. Moisture enters through cracks, board gaps, and end-grain, becomes trapped under the paint film, and causes blistering and peeling. Similar mechanism to solid stain failure on decks.
failure_modes.prevention: Ensure wood MC < 15% before coating. Prime all surfaces including board edges and undersides where accessible. Maintain caulk at board-to-structure joints. Ensure proper ventilation under porch floor. Covered porches have lower risk than open areas.
failure_modes.detection: Paint blistering and peeling on wood porch boards. Worst at board edges and end-grain. Moisture staining visible when paint is scraped.

failure_modes.name: Slip hazard from omitted anti-slip aggregate
failure_modes.description: Smooth coating applied to exterior porch/patio floor without anti-slip aggregate creates a dangerous slip hazard when wet. Exterior horizontal surfaces get wet from rain, snow, irrigation, and tracked moisture. DCOF drops below 0.55 on smooth coatings when wet — this is a safety and liability issue.
failure_modes.prevention: Add anti-slip aggregate to final coat on ALL exterior horizontal surfaces. Silica sand for level walkways, aluminum oxide for steps and ramps. Verify DCOF >= 0.55 on completed surface. This is an auto-add task, not optional.
failure_modes.detection: Slippery surface when wet. No visible texture in coating. DCOF test < 0.55.

notes_for_materials_manager: Dual-substrate spec — material systems branch on substrate_type (concrete vs wood).
CONCRETE — Porch enamel: alkali-resistant masonry primer (SW Loxon or equivalent) + acrylic porch & floor enamel. Coverage: 300-400 SF/gal on smooth concrete.
CONCRETE — Acrylic sealer: self-priming on properly profiled concrete. Coverage: 200-300 SF/gal (penetrates into pores).
CONCRETE — Concrete stain: acid stain or water-based stain + clear acrylic topcoat sealer. Coverage varies by porosity.
CONCRETE — Polyurea: manufacturer-specific primer/basecoat + polyurea topcoat. Coverage per manufacturer PDS. Typically 2-component, short pot life.
WOOD — Porch enamel: exterior wood primer (or alkyd primer for tannin-rich species) + acrylic or alkyd porch & floor enamel. Coverage: 350-400 SF/gal on smooth wood.
Anti-slip aggregate is a separate consumable: silica sand (30-60 mesh) for level surfaces, aluminum oxide (36-60 grit) for steps/ramps. Broadcast rate: 1-2 lbs per 100 SF.
Acid etch supplies: muriatic acid (or phosphoric acid alternative), neutralizer, PPE. Diamond grind is equipment rental, not material.
Moisture-mitigating primer as contingency material — triggered by MVER/RH hard stop.
Epoxy is EXCLUDED from v1 coating systems — do not include epoxy material systems.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Module structure: setup -> protect -> moisture_test (concrete only) -> prep -> prime -> apply -> anti_slip -> cleanup -> teardown.
CONCRETE prep module branches by coating_system: acid etch for stains/thin acrylics, diamond grind for porch enamel/polyurea.
WOOD prep module: mill glaze removal (chemical or 60-80 grit sand) + MC verification + light sand.
Moisture testing module is MANDATORY for concrete before any coating. MVER > 5 lbs OR RH > 85% = HARD STOP.
Anti-slip aggregate task is auto-add for ALL exterior floor specs. Aluminum oxide on steps/ramps, silica sand on level surfaces.
Concrete prime: alkali-resistant primer for porch enamel system; self-priming for acrylic sealer; manufacturer primer for polyurea.
Wood prime: exterior wood primer on bare wood. 2 finish coats of porch enamel.
Spray on concrete floors = ALWAYS add backroll (same as masonry). Spray-only NOT acceptable.
Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, surface temp) are SOP procedure notes — document go/no-go thresholds but these are NOT estimation modifiers.
Polyurea has short pot life — SOP must address batch mixing timing and application window.
Concrete stain requires clear topcoat sealer as separate task after stain cures.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Primary input: PS_EXT_SURFACE_SF.PORCH_FLOOR (total SF of porch/patio floor area).
CONCRETE PREP rates: acid etch ~200-400 SF/hr (manual), diamond grind 500-1,000 SF/hr (equipment), shot blast 1,500-3,000 SF/hr (rarely needed for residential).
CONCRETE COATING rates: porch enamel roll 150-250 SF/hr, acrylic sealer roll 200-300 SF/hr, polyurea roll 200-350 SF/hr (fast cure allows rapid recoat).
WOOD PREP rates: mill glaze sand 40-60 SF/hr, chemical mill glaze remover 100-150 SF/hr.
WOOD COATING rates: porch enamel brush/roll 100-150 SF/hr (brush edges, roll field).
Anti-slip aggregate broadcast: 300-500 SF/hr (broadcast into wet final coat).
Step detail work: 2-4 steps/hr (each tread is a separate unit with edge detail and aggregate).
Moisture testing: 0.5-1 hr per test location (ASTM F1869 requires 72-hr cure for calcium chloride test — this is a SCHEDULING item, not a production rate item).
Environmental conditions are EXCLUDED from estimation — SOP/process concerns only.
No height modifier for porch floors — crew works from the surface being coated. Ground-level access is the baseline.
Covered porch vs open patio does NOT change production rates — it affects coating system recommendation and maintenance cycle only.

Coat system: 1 primer + 2 finish coats for porch enamel (both substrates). Acrylic sealer: 2 coats (no primer on profiled concrete). Polyurea: per manufacturer (typically 1 primer + 1-2 topcoats). Concrete stain: 1-2 stain coats + 1-2 sealer topcoats.

zones.notes: LF-based — measured along porch perimeter where walls/siding meet the floor. Tape and paper/plastic at wall-floor junction to protect siding and foundation from floor coating splatter and roller spray.
LF-based — tape/paper at railing post bases where they meet the floor surface. Prevents floor coating from running onto railing posts.
EA-based — each door opening onto the porch. Mask threshold, door bottom, and weather strip to prevent coating contact.
LF-based — drop cloth or plastic along porch/patio edge where it meets landscape beds. Prevents acid etch runoff and coating drips from reaching plantings.
LF-based — tape/paper along porch/patio edge where it meets adjacent walkway, driveway, or other hardscape. Prevents coating from bleeding onto adjacent surfaces.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Railing painting is NOT this spec's responsibility — railing protection at the base is to prevent FLOOR coating from reaching railings. If railings are being painted, that is a separate spec (SF_DECK_EXT_v1 railing components or future porch railing spec). Door and window protection beyond the threshold belongs to their respective specs.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: House siding meets porch floor at wall-floor junction. Different coating systems. Protection tape at junction. Separate siding spec.
Foundation wall below porch floor level. Not painted in this scope. Protection at junction if applicable.
Railing posts sit on floor surface. Separate coating scope. Protection at post bases during floor coating.
Covered porch ceiling is overhead — no physical contact with floor. Separate soffit/ceiling spec. No protection needed (floor coating does not reach ceiling).
Floor coating terminates at door threshold. Clean cut-in line required. Threshold itself is masked/protected.
Floor coating terminates at porch-to-walkway transition. Clean edge line required. Adjacent hardscape protected with tape/paper.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Porch floor is a bounded horizontal surface with well-defined edges. Edge work is required at walkway transitions and door thresholds. All adjacent vertical surfaces (walls, railings, foundation) are separate specs with protection-only relationships.

values.covered_porch: Reduced UV/water exposure — standard coatings adequate
values.open_patio: Full weather exposure — premium coatings recommended

affected_conditions.notes: Affects recommendation and maintenance cycle expectation. Does not change task structure or production rates.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions are important to the painting PROCESS but are NOT estimatable at bid time. They belong in SOP procedure notes, not production rate modifiers. Height modifier is excluded because porch floor work is ground-level — crew stands on the surface being coated.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Cannot set a fixed modifier for estimate.
Varies by time of day, sun angle, and season. Not predictable at bid time.
Weather-dependent. Not predictable at bid time.
Not applicable — porch floor work is ground-level. No elevation access required.

valid_input_states.rationale: NC spec — only bare substrate states. SS_EXT_BARE_MASONRY covers new poured concrete porch/patio floors. SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD covers new wood porch decking. Repaint states (previously coated) would be a separate spec with fundamentally different prep requirements.

output_state.rationale: Output state varies by coating system: porch enamel produces a painted finish, acrylic sealer produces a sealed surface, concrete stain produces a stained+sealed surface, polyurea produces a coated surface. All include anti-slip texture.

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Protect finished siding from floor coating splatter. Unfinished siding will be painted later — floor work is typically early in NC sequence.
Protect finished railing post bases from floor coating. Unfinished railings will be painted later.

exterior_substrate_states.description: New poured concrete porch or patio floor. Alkaline surface (pH 12-14). May have laitance, form-release agents, or curing compounds on surface.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Remove laitance, form-release agents, oils, curing compounds. Achieve correct CSP per coating system (acid etch for CSP 1, diamond grind for CSP 2-3). Perform moisture testing (ASTM F1869 and/or F2170). Fill cracks and level low spots.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Alkali-resistant masonry primer for porch enamel system. Self-priming for acrylic sealer. Manufacturer-specific primer for polyurea. Concrete stain requires no primer (penetrating).
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Primary NC state. Concrete must be minimum 7 days cured (28 days ideal). Accelerated coating at 7 days requires alkali-resistant primer. Moisture testing is mandatory — MVER > 5 lbs or RH > 85% is a hard stop.

exterior_substrate_states.description: New wood porch decking — typically tongue-and-groove fir, pine, or pressure-treated pine. Has mill glaze from planing. May be green (unseasoned) if recently installed.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Remove mill glaze (chemical remover or 60-80 grit sanding). Verify MC < 15% (electronic pin meter). If PT pine, verify minimum 3 months seasoning. Light sand for adhesion profile.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: Exterior wood primer (acrylic or alkyd). Alkyd primer recommended for tannin-rich species (cedar, redwood).
exterior_substrate_states.notes: NC state. PT pine seasoning < 3 months is a HARD STOP — do not coat. Mill glaze removal is mandatory regardless of coating system.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers.

sop_reference_only.go_threshold: < 15 mph (floor-level work is less wind-sensitive than vertical spray)

sop_reference_only.go_range: 50-90°F concrete surface temperature. Below 50°F: slow cure. Above 90°F: flash dry, bubbling.
sop_reference_only.note: Dark concrete in direct sun can exceed 140°F — measure surface temp, not air temp.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5°F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Morning dew on porch floors is common — wait until surface is dry.

sop_reference_only.rule: Wood MC < 15% by electronic pin meter
sop_reference_only.note: Hard stop. Do not coat wet wood.

sop_reference_only.rule: Minimum 7 days cure (28 days ideal) for new concrete
No rain within 24-48 hours of application for most coatings
sop_reference_only.note: Polyurea has shorter rain-free window (4-6 hours) due to fast cure.

production_rate_research.source: Exterior_Concrete_Masonry_Floors_Doctrine.md; Exterior_Decks_Horizontal_Wood_Doctrine.md; calibrated against sibling specs SF_MASONRY_EXT_NC_v1 and SF_DECK_EXT_v1

concrete_acid_etch.notes: Manual process. Acid application, scrub, neutralize, rinse. Rate varies by area size and access.

concrete_diamond_grind.notes: Equipment-assisted. Walk-behind grinder. Higher end for open, unobstructed areas.

concrete_shot_blast.notes: Heavy equipment. Rarely needed for residential porch/patio. Included for completeness.

porch_enamel_roll_concrete.notes: Roll application on concrete. 3/8-1/2 inch nap for smooth, 3/4 inch for broom finish.

porch_enamel_brush_roll_wood.notes: Brush edges, roll field. Wood porch floor with T&G boards requires brush at board gaps.

acrylic_sealer_roll.notes: Thin application, fast dry. Two coats typical.

polyurea_roll.notes: Fast application, fast cure. Short pot life requires efficient workflow.

concrete_stain_apply.notes: Acid stain is slower (reactive process). Water-based stain is faster.

anti_slip_broadcast.notes: Broadcast aggregate into wet final coat. Fast operation.

step_detail.notes: Each tread: mask riser, apply coating, broadcast aggregate, detail nosing edge.

moisture_test_setup.notes: Per test location. ASTM F1869 calcium chloride requires 72-hr cure — scheduling item, not production rate.

crack_fill_patch.notes: Fill cracks with concrete patching compound. Rate depends on crack severity.

wood_mill_glaze_sand.notes: 60-80 grit mechanical sanding. Slower than chemical but more thorough.

wood_primer_roll.notes: Roll primer on sanded wood porch floor.

key_decisions.topic: Epoxy excluded from v1 coating systems
key_decisions.decision: Epoxy systems are EXCLUDED from this spec's coating_system dimension. Only porch_enamel, concrete_stain, acrylic_sealer, and polyurea are included.
key_decisions.rationale: Aromatic epoxies yellow and chalk under UV exposure — they are fundamentally an interior floor coating. Exterior use requires UV-stable topcoat (polyurethane or polyaspartic), adding complexity for minimal benefit. Polyurea provides superior performance for exterior residential without the UV limitation. Epoxy + topcoat is an industrial/commercial system outside this spec's residential scope.

key_decisions.topic: Scope limited to porch/patio — driveways and pool decks excluded
key_decisions.decision: This spec covers residential porch floors and patio surfaces (pedestrian walking surfaces only). Driveways and pool decks are EXCLUDED.
key_decisions.rationale: Driveways introduce hot tire pickup as a dominant failure mode requiring specialized polyurea or high-solids epoxy. Pool decks have chemical exposure (chlorine, salt) and enhanced slip resistance requirements. Both are distinct scopes warranting separate specs. Keeping this spec focused on walking surfaces maintains clear scope boundaries.

key_decisions.topic: Dual-substrate design — concrete and wood in one spec
key_decisions.decision: Both concrete and wood porch substrates are covered in a single spec with substrate_type as the primary branch dimension.
key_decisions.rationale: A porch floor is a porch floor regardless of substrate. The PaintScope key PS_EXT_SURFACE_SF.PORCH_FLOOR captures the surface area. Substrate_type branches the prep module, primer, and coating system. This avoids creating two nearly-identical specs (SF_PORCH_FLOOR_CONCRETE_EXT_NC_v1 and SF_PORCH_FLOOR_WOOD_EXT_NC_v1) that share protection zones, adjacency, and scope definition.

key_decisions.topic: Coating system as primary dimension instead of quality tier
key_decisions.decision: coating_system (porch_enamel, concrete_stain, acrylic_sealer, polyurea) is the primary configuration dimension. Quality tier is subordinate.
key_decisions.rationale: Coating system drives fundamentally different prep methods, primer requirements, application techniques, cure times, and maintenance cycles. Quality tier modifies execution precision within a given system (e.g., edge cleanness, DFT consistency) but does not change the workflow structure. This matches the deck spec (SF_DECK_EXT_v1) pattern where coating_type replaces quality_tier.

key_decisions.topic: Anti-slip aggregate is auto-add, not optional
key_decisions.decision: Anti-slip aggregate application is a MANDATORY auto-add task for ALL coating systems on exterior porch/patio floors. It is not an optional upgrade.
key_decisions.rationale: ANSI DCOF >= 0.55 is required for exterior wet areas. All exterior porch and patio surfaces get wet. Omitting anti-slip aggregate creates a slip hazard and liability exposure. This is a safety requirement, not an aesthetic choice.

key_decisions.topic: Moisture testing as a scheduling item, not a production rate item
key_decisions.decision: Moisture testing (ASTM F1869, F2170) is included as a task but recognized as primarily a scheduling concern rather than a production rate driver.
key_decisions.rationale: ASTM F1869 calcium chloride test requires 72-hour cure period. The actual labor to set up and read the test is 0.5-1 hour, but the 72-hour wait affects project scheduling. This is captured in SOP as a scheduling note, not as a production rate modifier.

key_decisions.decision: Height modifier (FAC_EXT_ACCESS) is NOT applicable to porch floor coating. All work is performed from the surface being coated.
key_decisions.rationale: Unlike siding or fascia work, porch floor coating is performed while standing on or adjacent to the work surface. There is no elevation access required. The crew is at ground level throughout. This is a departure from the siding/masonry sibling specs where access type drives a height modifier.

key_decisions.decision: Porch enamel (porch & floor paint) is available for BOTH concrete and wood substrates. It is the only coating system that crosses the substrate_type branch.
key_decisions.rationale: Porch enamel is the traditional residential porch floor treatment regardless of substrate material. On concrete it requires alkali-resistant primer; on wood it requires wood primer. But the finish coating itself and the application method are the same. This simplifies the spec — porch_enamel is the default/standard option for both paths.

key_decisions.topic: Concrete stain requires separate topcoat sealer task
key_decisions.decision: Concrete stain (acid or water-based) is a decorative penetrating product that requires a separate clear acrylic topcoat sealer for protection and slip resistance.
key_decisions.rationale: Penetrating concrete stains have no film formation and no abrasion resistance. Without a topcoat sealer, the stain would erode rapidly on a walking surface and anti-slip aggregate would have no binder to adhere to. The topcoat sealer is a separate task and separate material from the stain itself.

key_decisions.decision: Combined spec with full phase_scope. Primer and finish phases have unique task keys within the single spec.
key_decisions.rationale: Porch floor coating is a single-mobilization scope — same crew preps, primes, and coats. No reason to split into separate prime and finish specs. Each phase has its own task IDs and module IDs for independent tracking.

proposed_new_keys.description: Total square footage of porch/patio floor area to be coated. Includes main floor field and step treads.
proposed_new_keys.rationale: Primary input for this spec. Not currently in the PaintScope Exterior Key Catalog.

proposed_new_keys.description: Number of porch/patio steps (each tread is 1 EA). Drives step detail tasks and anti-slip aggregate on step nosings.
proposed_new_keys.rationale: Steps have distinct production rates and mandatory aluminum oxide aggregate. Count needed for EA-based task estimation.

research_corrections.original_claim: Environmental conditions (wind, dew_point, sun_exposure, surface_temp) should be included as estimation modifiers
research_corrections.corrected_to: Environmental conditions are site-level, unpredictable at bid time, and belong in SOP procedure notes only. They are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers. This is a standard exterior correction applied across all exterior specs.

Landscape and hardscape perimeter protection is measured in LF (linear feet along the edge), not SF. You measure the run along the porch/patio perimeter, not the area of landscape beds or adjacent hardscape.

research_corrections.original_claim: NC substrate condition modifier should be included for assessing concrete/wood condition
research_corrections.corrected_to: Substrate condition modifier is EXCLUDED for NC specs. Condition assessment (cracking, spalling, deterioration severity) is a repaint-only concern. NC substrates are by definition new — their condition is known. This spec handles only SS_EXT_BARE_MASONRY and SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD.

research_corrections.original_claim: Epoxy with UV topcoat is a viable exterior coating option for residential porches
research_corrections.corrected_to: Epoxy is EXCLUDED from v1. While technically viable with a UV-stable topcoat, the complexity and cost of a two-component system with mandatory topcoat is not justified for residential porch/patio. Polyurea provides equivalent or superior performance without the UV limitation. Epoxy remains valid for interior garage floors (separate spec).
research_corrections.corrected_by: Spec Researcher per user brief constraints

research_corrections.original_claim: Driveway coating is in scope for this porch/patio floor spec
research_corrections.corrected_to: Driveways are EXCLUDED. Hot tire pickup is a dominant driveway failure mode that does not apply to pedestrian walking surfaces. Driveways warrant a separate SF_DRIVEWAY_EXT_v1 spec. This spec is scoped to porch and patio floors only.
research_corrections.corrected_by: Spec Researcher per user brief constraints

covered_topics: Four coating systems (porch_enamel, concrete_stain, acrylic_sealer, polyurea)
Surface preparation methods and CSP requirements
Moisture testing protocols and hard stop thresholds
Slip resistance standards and anti-slip aggregate requirements
Failure modes for both concrete and wood substrates
Protection zones for porch floor work
Production rates for all major tasks
Material coverage rates and consumable requirements
Substrate state analysis for NC scope
gaps: Stamped/textured decorative concrete — may have different prep requirements than smooth poured concrete. Rare in NC but possible.
Porch floor with radiant heat — heated slabs may affect moisture dynamics and coating adhesion. Edge case for NC.
Regional wood species variations — spec assumes PT pine as dominant; regional species (cypress, ipe) would need species-specific notes.
recommendations: Validate polyurea production rates against manufacturer PDS for specific residential products (e.g., Penntek, Polyaspartic Garage).
Consider adding a stamped_concrete modifier in a future version if field demand warrants it.
Field-calibrate porch enamel brush/roll rates on wood porches — T&G board gaps may slow production more than estimated.

this_spec_owns: Porch and patio floor surface coating (concrete and wood substrates)
Surface preparation (CSP profiling, mill glaze removal, crack filling)
Step tread coating and nosing detail
Primer application for both substrate types
adjacent_specs_own: Porch railing painting — SF_DECK_EXT_v1 (railing components) or future porch railing spec
House siding adjacent to porch — SF_SIDING_FIBERCEMENT_EXT_NC_v1 or SF_WOOD_SIDING_EXT_NC_PAINT_v1
Adjacent walkway/driveway coating — future separate specs
shared_boundaries: Wall-floor junction: this spec protects the wall; siding spec does not need to protect the floor
Railing post base: this spec protects the post; railing spec does not need to protect the floor
Door threshold: this spec masks the threshold; door spec does not need to protect the floor
